content: The evidence regarding the use of postmenopausal hormone therapy and its association with breast cancer risk is more consistent compared to premenopausal women, where findings are less conclusive. No significant associations were observed between adult weight gain and breast cancer risk. Associations with waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio were not significant but shifted to positive associations in studies that adjusted for BMI. No significant associations were found for hormone receptor-defined premenopausal breast cancers. In conclusion, further research is needed to better understand the impact of these factors on premenopausal and postmenopausal breast cancers, as well as their subtypes, across the lifespan. This includes addressing variations in study definitions, exclusions, and methodologies. Data from ten studies involving 17,390 participants showed that reallocating 30 minutes of sedentary time to light-intensity physical activity was associated with reductions in waist circumference, fasting insulin, and all-cause mortality risk, as well as an increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Replacing sedentary time with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) showed stronger associations, including reductions in BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, and all-cause mortality, along with increased high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. These findings suggest that replacing sedentary time with physical activity, particularly MVPA, has significant health benefits, especially for a broader range of risk markers. Data from 9 studies with 850,060 participants revealed that higher levels of physical activity, regardless of intensity, and less sedentary time were associated with substantially reduced risks of premature mortality. A non-linear dose-response pattern was observed, with the greatest benefits seen in middle-aged and older adults who engaged in higher levels of physical activity. A separate meta-analysis explored the threshold of daily sedentary time associated with increased all-cause mortality risk. Based on pooled data from over 1 million participants, a log-linear dose-response relationship was identified, with increased mortality risks becoming significant when sedentary time exceeded 7 hours per day in self-reported studies and 9 hours per day in device-based studies. These findings highlight the importance of minimizing sedentary behavior to reduce mortality risk. In older adults, a meta-analysis found that higher amounts of sedentary time were associated with elevated mortality risks. A log-linear dose-response relationship indicated that mortality risks became significant when total sedentary time exceeded approximately 9 hours per day. These results suggest that older adults should aim to reduce daily sitting time to improve health outcomes. Regarding colorectal cancer, a systematic review and meta-analysis examined the associations between physical activity, sedentary behavior, and cancer risk across different domains (occupational, recreational, transport, and household). The analysis found that higher levels of physical activity were associated with a reduced risk of colorectal cancer, while occupational sedentary behavior was linked to an increased risk. Promoting physical activity across various domains and reducing sedentary behavior in the workplace may be effective strategies for colorectal cancer prevention. Finally, a meta-analysis assessed whether sedentary behavior-related mortality risk could be offset by moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). The findings demonstrated that sedentary behavior was significantly associated with mortality, but this risk was attenuated with increasing levels of MVPA. The results suggest that engaging in sufficient MVPA can mitigate the adverse health effects of prolonged sedentary behavior, emphasizing the importance of incorporating physical activity into daily routines.
